title: Architecture analysis: Conversational Claude coordinator for dynamic agent orchestration
summary: Introduce a coordinator agent that understands tasks, determines workflows, and drives the orchestrator dynamically. The recommended approach (Option A: Embedded Coordinator) adds a COORDINATOR agent role with elevated gateway permissions and coordinator-specific tools (spawn agents, monitor message bus, advance/skip phases, escalate to humans). A new SSE-based MCP server acts as a thin stateless bridge between external Claude Code sessions and the coordinator. The coordinator operates in hybrid phase mode — existing phases are advisory, the coordinator can skip/reorder them freely. The orchestrator gains new APIs for flexible agent spawning outside rigid phase sequences. Implementation is phased: v1 delivers the coordinator agent + orchestrator API extensions + MCP server; async triggers follow in v2.

problem_statement.description: The current SDLC pipeline follows a rigid, fixed-phase sequence (REFINE → PLAN → IMPLEMENT → PR) driven by CLI commands and pre-configured dispatch logic. Every task traverses the same phases regardless of complexity. Phase transitions require explicit CLI invocation or GitHub Actions automation. The system cannot reason about task complexity, skip unnecessary phases, loop back after failures, or adapt workflows in real time. There is no conversational interface — all orchestration requires knowledge of egg-orch, egg-contract, and phase mechanics.

root_causes.title: Fixed phase sequencing with no adaptive routing
root_causes.description: PipelinePhase enum defines exactly four phases (REFINE, PLAN, IMPLEMENT, PR) traversed sequentially. Phase transitions are driven by explicit API calls (POST /pipelines/{id}/phase) with no logic to evaluate whether a phase should be skipped based on task characteristics. Dispatch decisions come from pre-configured contract orchestrator logic, not runtime assessment.

root_causes.title: No intelligent task assessment or workflow selection
root_causes.description: The dispatch system (PipelineDispatcher in orchestrator/dispatch.py) delegates to egg_contracts.Orchestrator which returns fixed DispatchDecision objects with agents_to_run and wave_number. There is no mechanism to evaluate task complexity and select an appropriate workflow (e.g., single-agent quick fix vs. full multi-agent pipeline). All tasks get the same treatment.

root_causes.title: No feedback loop or loopback capability
root_causes.description: When a tester finds an issue, the current system cannot automatically re-spawn the coder. The phase must complete, a human reviews, and a new review cycle starts from scratch. The message bus (#1027) enables in-flight communication but no agent has authority to act on messages by spawning new agents or redirecting the workflow.

root_causes.title: No conversational interface for task submission
root_causes.description: Tasks enter the system via CLI (egg-sdlc, egg-orch pipeline create) or GitHub Actions. There is no natural language interface where a user can describe a task and have the system determine the appropriate workflow. No MCP server exists to bridge external Claude Code sessions with the orchestrator.

root_causes.title: No coordinator role in the agent model
root_causes.description: The AgentRole enum has no COORDINATOR role. All existing roles are task-execution roles (CODER, TESTER, etc.) or review roles (REVIEWER_CODE, etc.). No role has cross-phase authority to spawn agents, skip phases, or make workflow decisions.

current_architecture.execution_model: Wave-based sequential execution via MultiAgentExecutor or concurrent execution via ConcurrentPhaseExecutor. Standard Tier 2: Wave 1 (Coder) → Wave 2 (Tester + Documenter parallel) → Wave 3 (Integrator). Concurrent mode spawns all agents simultaneously with consensus-based completion. Both modes operate within a single phase — no cross-phase agent spawning.
current_architecture.communication_model: Completion-time handoff data (orchestrator/handoffs.py) for wave-based mode. In-memory message bus (orchestrator/message_store.py) for concurrent mode with typed messages (PROGRESS, QUESTION, STATUS, AGENT_FAILED, HANDOFF). Messages are polled by agents via REST API. No external-facing message interface exists.
current_architecture.phase_model: Four fixed phases (REFINE → PLAN → IMPLEMENT → PR) with per-phase permissions enforced by gateway (gateway/phase_filter.py). Phase transitions require explicit API calls. HITL gates between phases require human approval. Phase permissions define allowed git/gh/egg-contract operations per phase.
current_architecture.agent_model: Roles defined in AgentRole enum (orchestrator/models.py:64-88). File access patterns per role defined in shared/egg_contracts/agent_roles.py. Gateway enforces role-based file restrictions at commit time (gateway/agent_restrictions.py). Agent instructions come from sandbox/.claude/rules/ templates merged into CLAUDE.md at container startup.

key_components.name: PipelinePhase enum
key_components.description: Defines the four fixed phases: REFINE, PLAN, IMPLEMENT, PR. No mechanism for dynamic phase selection or skipping.

key_components.name: AgentRole enum
key_components.description: Defines all agent roles. No COORDINATOR role exists. Roles are phase-specific (REFINER for refine, ARCHITECT for plan, CODER for implement).

key_components.name: Pipeline creation endpoint
key_components.description: POST /pipelines endpoint. Supports 'issue' and 'local' modes with PipelineConfig. No coordinator mode.

key_components.name: PhaseFilter
key_components.description: Enforces per-phase operation permissions. Current phases: refine, plan, implement, pr. No coordinator or cross-phase permission model.

key_components.name: ContainerSpawner
key_components.description: Spawns agent containers with gateway sessions, env vars, mounts, and network config. spawn_agent_container() accepts agent_role, pipeline_id, extra_env for extensibility.

key_components.name: Agent role definitions
key_components.description: FileAccessPattern definitions for each role. ARCHITECT example: can write .egg-state/drafts/ and .egg-state/agent-outputs/, blocked from source code and contracts.

key_components.name: MessageStore
key_components.description: In-memory thread-safe message storage for concurrent mode. Supports add, query with role filtering, and status. Cleared on phase transition.

key_components.name: ConcurrentPhaseExecutor
key_components.description: Spawns all agents simultaneously within a phase. Manages consensus, failure handling, and per-agent worktree isolation.

key_components.name: SSE streaming
key_components.description: Per-pipeline and unified multi-pipeline event streaming. EventBus pub/sub pattern. Foundation for MCP server real-time updates.

key_components.name: Agent instructions
key_components.description: Template-based instruction files (mission.md, environment.md, orchestrator.md, etc.) merged into CLAUDE.md at container startup. New coordinator.md would follow same pattern.

recommended_approach.title: Option A: Embedded Coordinator — coordinator as a privileged agent container within the existing orchestrator
recommended_approach.description: Add a COORDINATOR agent role that runs as a standard agent container with elevated permissions and coordinator-specific tools. The coordinator uses Claude in headless mode (claude --print), consistent with all existing agents. It interacts with the orchestrator via REST APIs to spawn agents, monitor progress, advance/skip phases, and escalate decisions. A new SSE-based MCP server runs as a sidecar alongside the orchestrator, bridging external Claude Code sessions to the coordinator. The orchestrator gains new API endpoints for flexible agent spawning and coordinator-driven workflow control.
recommended_approach.justification: This approach is the natural evolution of the current architecture. The coordinator is just another agent — but with elevated permissions and coordinator-specific tools. This preserves the security model (gateway enforcement), reuses all existing infrastructure (container spawning, message bus, consensus, SSE streaming), and requires no new services beyond the MCP sidecar. It follows the EGG200 convention of keeping LLM reasoning inside Claude Code sessions rather than making direct Anthropic API calls from infrastructure. Option B (separate service) was rejected for violating EGG200. Option C (host-level session) conflates the coordinator with the user's development environment and breaks security isolation.

components.name: COORDINATOR agent role
components.description: New agent role added to AgentRole enum with a dedicated AgentRoleDefinition in agent_roles.py. The coordinator has restricted file access (write only to .egg-state/agent-outputs/) but elevated orchestrator API permissions — it can spawn agents across phases, skip/reorder phases, and create HITL escalations. File access is intentionally minimal because the coordinator's job is decision-making, not code generation.

components.name: Orchestrator API extensions for coordinator-driven spawning
components.description: New REST endpoints that allow the coordinator to: (1) spawn an agent with custom context/instructions outside the fixed dispatch system, (2) skip or advance phases programmatically, (3) request a loopback (re-spawn an agent with new context based on results), (4) query detailed pipeline state for decision-making. These endpoints are restricted to the COORDINATOR role via gateway session validation. The existing dispatch system (PipelineDispatcher) remains unchanged for non-coordinator pipelines.

components.name: Coordinator gateway permissions
components.description: New permission model for the coordinator role. The coordinator operates in a 'coordinator' pseudo-phase that grants cross-phase operation permissions: git push (to persist state), egg-contract operations, and coordinator-specific API calls. The gateway's phase_filter.py gains a coordinator permission set. The coordinator cannot push to production branches or create PRs directly — it instructs the orchestrator which handles those via appropriate phase-bound agents.

components.name: MCP server (SSE-based sidecar)
components.description: A new SSE-based MCP server that runs as a sidecar process alongside the orchestrator. It exposes tools to external Claude Code sessions: submit_task (create coordinator pipeline from natural language), get_status (query task state), provide_input (supply human input for coordinator escalations), list_tasks (list active coordinator tasks), cancel_task (request cancellation). The MCP server is stateless — it proxies all requests to the orchestrator's REST API. SSE transport is chosen over stdio because: (1) the server must be reachable from any Claude Code session, (2) it persists independently of client sessions, (3) it supports async/unattended mode. The server uses the MCP protocol specification for tool definitions and follows the SSE transport pattern.

components.name: Coordinator agent instructions and prompt design
components.description: New instruction file (sandbox/.claude/rules/coordinator.md) that defines the coordinator's operating model. The coordinator receives: task description, issue context, available agent roles, orchestrator tool descriptions. Instructions follow 'prefer what over how' — the coordinator gets objectives and tools, not step-by-step procedures. The coordinator-to-agent instruction protocol follows 'orientation not pre-fetching' — passing task objectives, issue number, branch, and focus area rather than pre-fetched diffs or file contents. Dynamic per-task context is injected via extra_env in container spawning, not by modifying rule templates.

components.name: Coordinator workflow state persistence
components.description: The coordinator persists workflow decisions and state to the orchestrator via API calls, not in its own context window. Key decision points (agent spawned, phase skipped, loopback initiated, human escalated) are recorded as structured events in the pipeline state. If the coordinator session crashes, a new coordinator can be spawned that re-assesses from current orchestrator state (objectives + current state) rather than replaying prior reasoning. This builds on the existing pipeline state store (orchestrator/state_store.py) with a new 'coordinator_state' field on the Pipeline model.

components.name: Coordinator observability via message bus and SSE
components.description: New message types on the message bus for coordinator decisions: WORKFLOW_DECISION (phase skip/reorder), AGENT_SPAWN (coordinator requested agent), ESCALATION (human input needed), LOOPBACK (re-running agent). These are lightweight event emissions (subject + brief body) surfaced via the existing SSE stream and DAG visualizer. The coordinator's full session transcript is captured by the checkpoint system. No structured-output requirements are imposed on coordinator reasoning.

components.name: Pipeline mode: coordinator-driven execution
components.description: A new pipeline configuration flag (config.coordinator_enabled) that activates coordinator-driven execution. When enabled, the orchestrator spawns a coordinator agent as the first container instead of following the fixed phase dispatch. The coordinator then drives all subsequent agent spawning and phase transitions. The existing SDLC CLI and fixed-phase execution remain unchanged when coordinator_enabled is false (default). This is an opt-in mode that coexists with the existing pipeline model.

coordinator_tools.description: Spawn an agent container with a specific role, task context, and optional custom instructions. The coordinator passes task objectives and lightweight metadata (issue number, branch, focus area) — not pre-fetched diffs or file contents.
Query comprehensive pipeline state: phase, running agents, completed agents, pending decisions, message bus activity, health check results.
Advance the pipeline to the next phase or skip to a specific phase. The coordinator provides a reason for the transition.

Surface a question or decision to the human via HITL mechanism. Supports both multiple-choice decisions and open-ended feedback. Blocks until human responds (synchronous via MCP) or queues for async notification.
Send a message to a running agent via the message bus. Used for mid-execution redirection or additional context.
Poll the message bus for messages from running agents. Used to monitor progress and detect issues requiring coordinator intervention.
Request cancellation of a running agent container. Used when the coordinator decides an agent's work is no longer needed.

mcp_tools.description: Accept a natural language task description and optional metadata (issue number, repo, urgency). Creates a coordinator-enabled pipeline and spawns the coordinator agent. Returns a task ID for status tracking.
Query current state of a coordinator-managed task: which agents are running, what phase, pending decisions, recent coordinator decisions.
Supply human input in response to a coordinator escalation. Can be a decision selection or free-form text.
List active and recent coordinator-managed tasks with summary status.
Request cancellation of a coordinator-managed task. Stops all running agents and marks the pipeline as cancelled.

alternatives_considered.title: Option B: External Coordinator Service
alternatives_considered.description: Build a standalone coordinator service that manages a Claude session via direct Anthropic API calls and translates high-level decisions into orchestrator API calls.
pros: Clean separation of concerns — orchestrator manages execution, coordinator manages decisions
Can manage multiple pipelines simultaneously from a single service
Custom session persistence without container lifecycle constraints
cons: Violates EGG200 convention — makes direct Anthropic API calls from infrastructure code, bypassing the sandbox boundary
New service to build, deploy, and maintain
Must duplicate or proxy orchestrator functionality
Requires its own credential management for Anthropic API
alternatives_considered.rejected_reason: Violates the EGG200 convention that LLM reasoning happens inside Claude Code sessions, not via programmatic API calls from orchestration services (per docs/guides/agent-mode-design.md). This is a fundamental architectural principle, not a minor guideline.

alternatives_considered.title: Option C: Host-Level Claude Code Session
alternatives_considered.description: The coordinator runs as a Claude Code session on the host using existing tools plus coordinator-specific skills. It interacts with the orchestrator via egg-orch CLI commands.
pros: Leverages Claude Code's native tool system and context management
Natural conversation interface — user interacts directly with Claude Code
Can directly read repository context without container indirection
cons: Runs outside the sandbox security boundary
May conflict with existing Claude Code session
Depends on Claude Code-specific features that may change
alternatives_considered.rejected_reason: Conflates the coordinator with the user's development environment. Option A can evolve into a host-level mode later if desired, but the foundation should be container-based for security isolation and portability.

technical_decisions.title: Coordinator runs as agent container, not standalone service
technical_decisions.decision: The coordinator is a standard agent container with the COORDINATOR role, spawned by the orchestrator. It uses claude --print in headless mode, consistent with all existing agents.
technical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the security model (gateway enforcement), reuses container infrastructure (spawning, monitoring, checkpointing), and follows EGG200 convention. The coordinator is 'just another agent' with elevated permissions.
technical_decisions.trade_offs: Container overhead while coordinator is running. Claude context window limits session lifetime (~200k tokens). Mitigated by checkpoint/resume from orchestrator state.

technical_decisions.title: MCP server uses SSE transport, runs as orchestrator sidecar
technical_decisions.decision: The MCP server uses SSE (Server-Sent Events) transport and runs alongside the orchestrator, sharing the same network. It is stateless — all state lives in the orchestrator.
technical_decisions.rationale: SSE allows multiple Claude Code sessions to connect independently. The server persists across client disconnections. It naturally maps to the orchestrator's HTTP architecture and supports the async/unattended mode where no Claude Code session is active. Stateless design means crash recovery is trivial.
technical_decisions.trade_offs: Network dependency between Claude Code and MCP server. SSE requires HTTP infrastructure. Alternative: stdio transport is simpler but requires co-located processes.

technical_decisions.title: Hybrid phase model — phases are advisory for coordinator
technical_decisions.decision: The existing phase system (REFINE → PLAN → IMPLEMENT → PR) remains but is advisory when coordinator_enabled is true. The coordinator can skip, reorder, or combine phases. Gateway permissions for the coordinator use a 'coordinator' pseudo-phase that grants cross-phase operation access.
technical_decisions.rationale: Preserves backward compatibility — non-coordinator pipelines use the existing fixed-phase model unchanged. The coordinator gets flexibility without breaking the structural guarantees that phases provide for other agents. The 'coordinator' pseudo-phase is a clean extension point in gateway/phase_filter.py.
technical_decisions.trade_offs: Two execution models (fixed-phase and coordinator-driven) add complexity. Gateway permission model becomes more nuanced. Mitigated by keeping the coordinator pseudo-phase permissions minimal and well-documented.

technical_decisions.title: Coordinator-to-agent instructions follow orientation-not-prefetching
technical_decisions.decision: The coordinator passes agents task objectives, issue number, branch name, and a brief focus description — not pre-fetched diffs, file contents, or detailed step-by-step procedures. Dynamic context is injected via extra_env in container spawning.
technical_decisions.rationale: Per agent-mode design guidelines (docs/guides/agent-mode-design.md), agents should receive orientation (what to accomplish) rather than pre-fetched context (here's the code to change). Agents are capable of gathering their own context. Pre-fetching wastes coordinator tokens and creates stale-context risks.
technical_decisions.trade_offs: Agents must spend tokens gathering context themselves. For very targeted tasks, pre-fetched context could save agent time. Mitigated by providing clear, specific task objectives that help agents focus their context gathering.

technical_decisions.title: Coordinator state persists in orchestrator, not context window
technical_decisions.decision: Workflow decisions, agent spawn history, phase transitions, and escalation history are persisted as structured state in the orchestrator's Pipeline model (new coordinator_state field). A crashed coordinator re-assesses from this state rather than replaying prior reasoning.
technical_decisions.rationale: Claude's context window (~200k tokens) is insufficient for multi-hour workflows with many tool calls. Persisting state externally means the coordinator can be restarted without losing progress. The orchestrator's git-backed state store already provides reliable persistence.
technical_decisions.trade_offs: State serialization/deserialization overhead. Coordinator must reconstruct reasoning context from state on resume. Mitigated by keeping state structured and including enough context for re-assessment.

technical_decisions.title: Opt-in coordinator mode via PipelineConfig flag
technical_decisions.decision: Coordinator-driven execution is activated by setting config.coordinator_enabled=true on pipeline creation. Default is false. The existing SDLC CLI and fixed-phase pipelines are completely unaffected.
technical_decisions.rationale: Zero risk of breaking existing workflows. Users can adopt the coordinator incrementally. The MCP server's submit_task tool creates pipelines with coordinator_enabled=true automatically. CLI users can opt in with --coordinator flag.
technical_decisions.trade_offs: Two execution paths to maintain. Over time, the coordinator mode may become the default and the fixed-phase mode may be deprecated. But maintaining both during the transition period ensures stability.

risks.title: Coordinator session lifetime vs. multi-hour workflows
risks.description: Claude's context window (~200k tokens) and conversation limits may be insufficient for coordinator sessions that manage complex, multi-hour workflows with many agent spawns and interactions.
risks.mitigation: Persist all workflow state in orchestrator. Design coordinator prompts to be compact. Implement checkpoint/resume: when context approaches limits, the coordinator saves state and a new session is spawned that reconstructs context from orchestrator state. The coordinator re-assesses rather than replays.

risks.title: Runaway agent spawning
risks.description: A coordinator in a failure loop could repeatedly spawn agents (coder fails → spawn coder → fails again → spawn coder → ...), consuming significant compute and cost.
risks.mitigation: Implement guardrails: max agents per task (configurable, default 10), max retry count per role (default 2), max wall-clock time per coordinator session (configurable), max total token budget. The orchestrator enforces these limits and terminates the coordinator if exceeded.

risks.title: Gateway permission model complexity
risks.description: The coordinator's cross-phase permission model adds complexity to the gateway's phase_filter.py. The 'coordinator' pseudo-phase must be carefully scoped to avoid granting excessive permissions.
risks.mitigation: Coordinator permissions are minimal: write only to .egg-state/agent-outputs/, orchestrator API calls for spawning and phase management. The coordinator cannot push to production branches, create PRs, or modify source code directly. All dangerous operations are performed by appropriately phase-bound agents spawned by the coordinator.

risks.title: MCP server as new attack surface
risks.description: The MCP server exposes orchestrator capabilities over HTTP. If accessible from untrusted networks, it could be used to submit unauthorized tasks or manipulate running pipelines.
risks.mitigation: MCP server listens only on the egg-isolated network (172.32.0.0/24). Authentication via gateway session tokens. Rate limiting on task submission. The MCP server is a thin proxy — all authorization is enforced by the orchestrator and gateway.

risks.title: Coordinator crash with running agents
risks.description: If the coordinator crashes mid-workflow, running agents may complete without a coordinator to process their results or spawn follow-up agents.
risks.mitigation: Running agents continue and auto-commit (existing post-agent auto-commit behavior). The orchestrator detects coordinator container exit and can either: (1) spawn a new coordinator to re-assess, or (2) notify the human. Workflow state in orchestrator allows the new coordinator to pick up where the old one left off.

risks.title: Dual execution model maintenance burden
risks.description: Maintaining both fixed-phase and coordinator-driven execution models increases codebase complexity and testing surface.
risks.mitigation: The coordinator mode reuses most existing infrastructure (container spawning, gateway, message bus). New code is concentrated in coordinator-specific files (coordinator_executor.py, mcp_server.py, mcp_tools.py, coordinator.md). The fixed-phase codepath is unchanged — no dual-maintenance of core logic.

dependencies.title: Cross-agent communication (#1027)
dependencies.description: Message bus, consensus protocol, concurrent execution, per-agent worktrees. Foundation for coordinator monitoring and agent communication.

dependencies.title: HITL decisions from refine phase
dependencies.description: Four unresolved HITL decisions (session persistence, phase model, coordinator authority, implementation scope) and three feedback questions (cost guardrails, failure recovery, multi-task coordination). These decisions influence the plan but the architect analysis provides recommendations that can be adjusted when decisions are resolved.

implementation_phases.title: Core coordinator + orchestrator APIs + MCP server
implementation_phases.description: COORDINATOR role, orchestrator API extensions, gateway permissions, coordinator instructions, MCP server with SSE transport, coordinator executor, workflow state persistence, observability. This delivers the full interactive workflow: user submits task via MCP → coordinator analyzes → spawns agents → monitors → escalates → completes.

implementation_phases.title: Async triggers and unattended mode
implementation_phases.description: Slack integration, webhook triggers, GitHub issue event triggers for coordinator-driven workflows without a live Claude Code session. Notification channels for async escalation. This is explicitly marked as follow-on in the issue.

open_questions_for_planner.question: How should the coordinator handle concurrent agent failures? Should it implement circuit-breaker logic (stop spawning after N failures) or always escalate to human?
open_questions_for_planner.recommendation: Circuit-breaker with configurable threshold (default: 2 consecutive failures of same role → escalate). This prevents runaway loops while allowing recovery from transient failures.

open_questions_for_planner.question: Should the MCP server support real-time streaming of coordinator decisions (via SSE to Claude Code), or is polling sufficient for v1?
open_questions_for_planner.recommendation: Polling for v1. The MCP server already uses SSE transport for the protocol itself. Real-time streaming of coordinator decisions is a nice-to-have that can be added in v2 by connecting the MCP server to the orchestrator's EventBus.

open_questions_for_planner.question: How should the coordinator communicate task-specific instructions to spawned agents beyond environment variables?
open_questions_for_planner.recommendation: Use extra_env for lightweight metadata (issue number, branch, focus area). For richer context, the coordinator writes a task brief to .egg-state/agent-outputs/{issue}-coordinator-brief.json which spawned agents read at startup. This follows orientation-not-prefetching: the brief contains objectives and constraints, not pre-fetched code.

open_questions_for_planner.question: What is the coordinator's relationship to the existing contract system (egg-contract)?
open_questions_for_planner.recommendation: The coordinator creates and manages contracts for the tasks it spawns, using the same egg-contract CLI. For coordinator-driven pipelines, the contract may be simpler (fewer rigid phase gates) but still tracks tasks, commits, and decisions for auditability.
